text: FINDING, caught by SW-044's own hand-back within a minute of shipping it. done() computes `dirty` from `git status --porcelain` over the whole tree. But .shipward/tracker.json is version-controlled here BY DESIGN — git is the authority, so the board is committed — and the MCP server rewrites mcp.lastSeen into it every 60 seconds as a heartbeat. The tracker file is therefore ALWAYS modified while a session is open. Measured at 10:46 on 2026-07-31: SW-044's check passed at 4ecfeaf with exactly one dirty path, `.shipward/tracker.json`, and nothing else. The consequence is not cosmetic: dirty:true makes freshness() report `unanchored` at birth, permanently, so no evidence this product ever writes can be current and the whole of SW-044 renders one state forever. SW-043's dirty caveat is equally defeated — it fires on every card and therefore says nothing. FIX, small: the tree that matters is the code under test, not the board describing it. Exclude .shipward/ when computing `dirty` in headState() — `git status --porcelain -- ':(exclude).shipward/'` or filter the porcelain lines — and say in the comment WHY the exclusion is honest rather than convenient: a tracker write is not a change to the thing the check exercised. Consider also whether the heartbeat belongs in tracker.json at all; mcp.mjs already records that tradeoff as chosen deliberately (one file occasionally dirty beat two files that can disagree), and this is the first real cost of it. Do NOT fix by dropping the dirty flag: a pass over genuinely uncommitted source is exactly the claim it exists to qualify.

FIXED, and this hand-back is the proof: the heartbeat had already rewritten mcp.lastSeen into tracker.json before the check ran — the exact condition that made SW-044's evidence dirty an hour ago — and this check recorded dirty:false. headState() now excludes .shipward/ when deciding whether the tree is dirty. The reasoning is written at the call site so nobody reads it as convenience: a write to the BOARD is not a change to the thing the check exercised, while uncommitted SOURCE still counts, because that is the claim the flag exists to qualify. SECOND BUG FOUND WHILE FIXING THE FIRST, and it was latent in SW-043 from the start: the old code parsed `git status --porcelain` by column, but git() trims its own output, so the leading space of the FIRST line's two-character status field was already gone and that one path came back short by a character. Always the first entry, never the rest, and nothing would have caught it because dirty was only ever read as a boolean. Replaced with bare-path queries — `diff --name-only HEAD` plus `ls-files --others --exclude-standard` — which have no columns to misread. headState now also returns dirtyPaths (capped at 10), because 'dirty' with nothing to point at is a claim a reader cannot check. 335 tests pass, five of them new and specifically about this: board-only change is clean, source change is dirty, untracked source is dirty, a staged path is exact rather than off by one, and a board change ALONGSIDE a source change is still dirty.

FOUND WHILE starting SW-039 on 2026-07-31: `git diff` on shipward/tracker-store.mjs prints "Binary files … differ" and shows nothing. git blame, code review and conflict resolution all degrade to nothing on it — and that file's own header comment enumerates eight separate lost-write bugs, so it is the last file in this repo whose changes should be unreviewable.

ROOT CAUSE, and it is NOT corruption: feedKey (line 79) was changed from .join(' ') to join on a NUL — a good hardening, since NUL cannot occur inside a timestamp, project id, author or message, so two entries can no longer collide by containing the separator. But it was written as a RAW NUL BYTE in the source rather than the escape. git's binary heuristic looks for a NUL in the first 8000 bytes; this one is at offset 4573, so the whole file is classified binary.

FIX is one character and semantically identical at runtime: write '\u0000' (or '\0') in the string literal instead of embedding the byte. The joined key is unchanged, so nothing about feed archiving changes.

Note for whoever picks this up: `grep` on this machine returns nothing at all (it is broken — verified 2026-07-31, it produced no output even for `grep -c ""`), so a NUL hunt with grep will report a clean file. Use node, or rg. That is also why this went unnoticed.

SHIPPED and pushed to main (c0d17b3). feedKey's NUL separator is now the escape form instead of an embedded byte — byte-identical at runtime, so no archived feed line changes. git classifies the file as text again, which is the whole point: shipward/tracker-store.mjs is the file whose header comment enumerates eight lost-write bugs, and its diffs were showing "Binary files differ".

FOUND WHILE starting SW-039 (which rewrites this file, so I needed its diffs readable).

GOTCHA worth keeping: git's binary heuristic only scans the first 8000 bytes, so this is silent for a NUL further in — and `grep` on this machine is broken (returns nothing for any pattern, verified with `grep -c ""`), so the usual NUL hunt reports a clean file. Use node or rg.

BRIEF. EnterWorktree and `git worktree add` both put worktrees under .claude/worktrees/, and .gitignore does not mention it — so `git status` on main shows an untracked directory containing a full second checkout, and one inattentive `git add -A` would commit it into the repo. Two are live right now (SW-043 and the concurrent session's bound-memory-reads). The fix is one line. Noted because the near-miss is not theoretical: this repo tracks 1,525 files under .claude/skills, so .claude is a directory people DO add wholesale.

SHIPPED to main. One line — `.claude/worktrees/` — plus the reason above it, because an ignore rule with no comment is the kind of line someone deletes while tidying. Committed straight to main rather than on a branch: switching branches in the shared checkout would have disturbed the concurrent session working out of it, and the change is one ignore line with no code path. Verified by the gate SW-043 added, which is the point of running it on something this small: the check ran against main's working tree while tracker.json was dirty with this very card's log entry, so the evidence records dirty:true and says it is not reproducible from the sha alone. That is the honest reading and it is what the caveat exists for.

FINDING, found while shipping SW-043. spawnCheck() does not set `env`, so the check inherits the server's environment — including SHIPWARD_TRACKER and SHIPWARD_REPO. A project whose check is its own test suite therefore runs that suite with a pointer to the LIVE board in the environment. This is the exact shape of the SW-033 incident, where a test sandbox resolved the real tracker through the cwd-first ladder and its PUT tests replaced 32 cards and 111 feed entries. It is not exploitable here today — the suite is proven byte-neutral against the real tracker, and that was re-verified by md5 before SW-043's own done() was allowed to run it — but the belt is a property of the suite, not of the runner, and the next repo to declare `checks: {default: [...]}` inherits no such proof. Options, cheapest first: scrub SHIPWARD_* from the child env (a check that genuinely needs them can be given them explicitly); or pass SHIPWARD_TRACKER pointing at a scratch copy; or leave it and say so in the docs. Decide before onboarding tells other repos to declare checks.

BRIEF. Decision taken 2026-07-31: open source this under MIT rather than trying to charge for it. Reasoning, so nobody reopens it cheaply — there is nothing to gate (local-first, zero-dep, no auth, readable ES modules; a licence check is a three-line delete), the competition is free AND bundled with the tool you already pay for (Claude Code shipped built-in Tasks in v2.1.16), and distribution in this niche is stars, HN and the Claude Code ecosystem, where closed source is not premium, it is invisible. The asset is the judgment (git-as-truth tiers, note epistemics), which only pays out if it can be read. Timing matters: publish while 'Tasks has no repo awareness, no web UI, no MCP server, no git integration' is still true — a comparable project went from side project to absorbed-by-the-platform in months. WORK, all verified against the repo on 2026-07-31: (1) there is NO LICENSE and NO README at all; (2) git tracks 1,525 files under .claude/skills plus 72 under _bmad, none of which carry a bundled LICENSE file — third-party scaffolding that must be stripped or its terms verified before publishing; (3) a 43KB 'App progress tracker prototypes.zip' is committed at the root; (4) the shippable product is 26 files in shipward/, 3 in .shipward/, and CLAUDE.md; (5) design_handoff_shipward/ came from Claude Design — check what may be redistributed; (6) .shipward/tracker.json is real working memory about ten of Alberto's projects, including the incident write-ups. Publishing it is the single best demo this project has — a live board with real notes beats any screenshot — but read it end to end first, because it is a publishing decision, not a code one. README should carry the measurement that answers the token argument: tools/list is 6,843 bytes (~1.7k tokens) for all six tools, measured 2026-07-31.

BRIEF. The four hooks are Claude Code specific, but the protocol is not — and today an agent that is not Claude Code has no cheap way in. Ship a thin CLI (shipward standup | log | start | done) over the same tracker-store and lib.js rules, so any agent that can run a shell command gets the protocol and any repo gets it without hook support. Cost is low: standup.mjs and status.mjs already run standalone by design. Secondary benefit — it strengthens an argument this project can already win. The standing argument against MCP for Claude Code is token cost — CLI+hooks recommended over MCP on the grounds of '~1-2k tokens vs 10-50k for MCP schemas'; measured 2026-07-31, this server's tools/list response is 6,843 bytes (~1.7k tokens) for all six tools, i.e. an MCP surface already at parity with a CLI. Worth stating in the README with the measurement, and worth a regression test so it stays true.

BRIEF. SW-038 shipped a regression that no test could have caught: the fleet page's origin validator rejected the new ?fleet= URLs and silently unlinked every board — ten rows, zero anchors, no error — and it surfaced only in the live browser. That card already recorded the known limit (zero-dep means no jsdom, so row rendering has no DOM-level test). Fix it in the grain of the codebase rather than by adding Playwright and losing the zero-dependency story: push markup generation into pure functions in lib.js that take data and return strings, and test those under node --test — the same move that made fleetLinkFrom() testable. The bug class to target is producer/consumer drift, which is precisely what a pure function pins.

BRIEF. fleet.mjs lists boards and spawns a desk per board; it does not yet answer anything that needs more than one board at a time. Add the aggregate view: one standup across every onboarded repo, what has been sitting in review longest anywhere, which repo has not shipped in N weeks, everything currently in flight. Mostly aggregation over the walk and the per-repo trackers that already exist. Strategic reason to prioritise it: cross-repo unification is the axis Alberto's 2026-07-10 sweep found agent-native tools worst at, AND it is the axis Claude Code's built-in Tasks structurally cannot reach — that system has no repo awareness and its task-list ids can collide across repos. Per-repo trackers (never pooled) plus a fleet that reads across them is the right shape and is already half-built.

BRIEF. The reported tier is defined in git.mjs and deliberately never written by anything automatic — which means the most interesting data in the system is currently invisible. Give it a desk surface: cards claiming pushed whose commit is nowhere on the trunk, branches no card claims, files changed with no card in flight, review cards ageing past N days, notes carrying no evidence entry at all. Nothing here writes to the board — it reports, and a human decides, which is exactly the tier's existing rule. Why it matters commercially: the actual pain of running an agent solo is not knowing what happened while you were away, and every competing tracker assumes the agent's report is true. This repo has the machinery to contradict it and does not yet show the contradiction to anyone.

SHIPPED as a fifth desk tab (Alberto ratified own-tab over an always-visible strip, and report-unverified-but-scoped over count-everything). The reported tier finally has a surface. FIVE RULES, THREE KINDS OF QUESTION, and keeping them apart underneath is the design: what git disproves (not-on-trunk, untracked-branch) is PASSED THROUGH from deriveFindings rather than re-derived, because two implementations of 'is this commit on the trunk' would eventually disagree and the desk would then contradict sync(); what board arithmetic shows (uncarded-changes, stale-review at 7 days) needs no git at all; what the memory is missing (never-verified) is new ground that only exists because SW-043 made evidence something a card can earn. THE DECISION WORTH KEEPING: never-verified is scoped to cards handed back AFTER checks began here, and that date is DERIVED — the earliest verification.at on the board — rather than stored. 51 cards predate verification; listing them would have opened the panel with fifty findings about the past, which teaches a reader to close it. A derived date also cannot drift from the thing it describes, which a stored one would. FIRST REAL FINDINGS, live: SW-040 and SW-041, both handed back by the concurrent session running pre-SW-043 code, so nothing ran. Correct, useful, and not something any other surface would have told anyone. No alarm colour anywhere — every row is a question a human answers, and unproven is not an accusation. KNOWN LIMIT, stated rather than papered over: only the never-verified rendering path was verified in a browser. An honest repo cannot currently produce the other four, a throwaway branch does not count as untracked-branch (deriveFindings measures commits ahead, not refs — correct behaviour, and worth knowing), and app.js's state is module-scoped so synthetic findings cannot be injected from the console. The rules have 18 unit tests; the markup for four of five categories has none. That is exactly SW-047's ground. 355 tests pass, up from 335.

BRIEF. standup.mjs already says evidence rots — the PERISHABLE caveat, 'as of then, not a claim about now'. Make it mechanical instead of textual: an evidence entry carries the sha it was written against, and git.mjs can answer whether that sha is still reachable from HEAD and whether the files the entry concerned have been touched since. Then recall({file}) stops reporting '252 tests pass' flatly and reports '252 tests passed at 1942e8c — N commits have touched this file since', and the desk fades a verified badge as the work drifts out from under it. Pairs with the verification-gating card, which is what starts stamping shas onto evidence in the first place; this card is cheap once that exists. Positioning value: 'memory that knows it is out of date' is a claim no competitor in this category makes, and it is the natural headline for the write-up.

SHIPPED. Evidence entries now carry the sha they were true of, and standup/recall/the desk all read one freshness() verdict over a driftSince() map that asks git once per DISTINCT sha. FOUR STATES, and the design point is that the two ways of NOT knowing are kept apart: a sha git cannot resolve is `unknown`, never `fresh`, because a rebased-away or foreign sha answering '0 commits since' would render as still-current — a confident lie, which is the exact failure this card exists to remove. DECIDED: evidence with no sha keeps the old PERISHABLE wording rather than getting a second phrase for the same fact; a caveat that changes when nothing has changed teaches a reader to ignore it. A dirty tree IS new information, so that one speaks for itself. THE BUG WORTH REMEMBERING, and it cost the most time here: inside the SessionStart hook I declared `let drift` for the drift map, but `drift` is ALREADY the name of the git-audit function called three lines earlier in the same scope — so that call hit the temporal dead zone and threw, and the hook's own catch-all (Rule 1: never break a session) turned the crash into SILENCE. SessionStart emitted nothing at all: no standup, no audit, no error, exit 0. Six hook tests went blank rather than red, which is what caught it. A shadowed binding plus a fail-open catch is an invisible outage; the variable is named driftMap and the reason is written above it. SCOPE NOTE: /api/drift polls on its own 60s timer, not the tracker's 3s — the answer changes when commits land, a few times a day, and spawning git twenty times a minute for it would be absurd. VERIFIED IN THE BROWSER, which is the part no test covers (see SW-047): the Memory tab rendered 35 badges on 35 evidence entries and zero on any other kind, all reading 'unanchored' at 0.55 opacity — correct, because every entry on the board predates sha stamping. This card's own hand-back writes the first anchored one. 330 tests pass, up from 302.

BRIEF. Strategy card, from a 2026-07-31 market read: Anthropic shipped built-in Tasks in Claude Code v2.1.16 (persistent via CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID, credited to a prior open-source tracker) and that tracker now has a community web dashboard. The 'what should I work on next' half of this category is commoditised. The half nobody owns is 'prove it was done'. Today done() accepts a claim: the note nudge asks for prose, nothing checks the work. Build: a card carries a `verify` command (e.g. `node --test`); done() runs it, captures exit code plus the head of the output, and writes an evidence entry stamped WITH THE SHA IT RAN AGAINST. Three outcomes mirroring the git tiers in git.mjs — verified (ran, passed, at this sha), unverified (no check declared, and it says so rather than implying success), refuted (ran, failed: done is refused or the card returns to claude with the failure in the note). This is the existing thesis extended one step: git outranks the claim about the commit, the test run outranks the claim about the work. Alberto's 2026-07-10 sweep of 69 agents found verification gating 'barely exists anywhere'; it still does not exist as of 2026-07-31. It is also the hardest thing here to copy, because it only means anything on top of the tier and provenance machinery already in git.mjs and reconcile.mjs. DECIDED NOT TO BUILD (same session): dependency DAG, ready-queries, leases, multi-agent coordination — that is the incumbent's engine and competing on it head-on with a zero-dep solo project loses.

SHIPPED, and this hand-back is its own first demonstration: the check that gated it is the one it added. Built as designed in _bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-verification-gating.md (ratified by Alberto before a line was written): checks are argv arrays declared by a HUMAN on the project, a card carries only a name, done() resolves and runs it, and the outcome is stamped with the sha and the cleanliness of the tree it ran on. TWO THINGS THE CODE CHANGED ABOUT THE SKETCH. (1) The check cannot run inside mutate(): mutate holds the cross-process advisory lock for the length of its callback and waiters give up at LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS=60000, so a suite inside one would not deadlock — it would starve the desk and every other session for as long as it takes. It runs unlocked between a read and a brief write, and a test pins the ordering by racing a standup against a 1.5s check. (2) A free-text verify command on a card is disqualifying: this file is written by an agent and by an unauthenticated PUT /api/tracker, so a command stored in it is an exec for anything that can write the tracker. Hence argv arrays, shell:false, and a card that can only SELECT. DECISION MADE DURING THE BUILD, not in the design: one rule for everything that was promised and did not pass — failed, timed out, could not spawn, OR named a check nobody declares. The first draft held the card on a timeout but promoted it on a typo, which would have made the gate optional by misspelling; that is the SW-038 failure mode (a feature silently doing nothing) wearing different clothes. WHAT A PASS CLAIMS, deliberately narrow: a declared command exited zero on a named tree. Not that the work is correct — the note says so in those words, because an agent that writes a passing test for broken code defeats this entirely. A pass over a dirty tree says that too, since it is not reproducible from the sha. 293 tests pass, up from 252: 33 new in verify.test.mjs (including the one that proves shell metacharacters are not interpreted and no file is created) and 8 in mcp.test.mjs. verification.sha is what SW-044 reads to expire this evidence; ok/at are what SW-045 counts. LEFT OPEN: the check inherits SHIPWARD_TRACKER from the server's environment — logged as its own card rather than buried here.

FOUND WHILE filing SW-039..041 on 2026-07-31, by reading standup’s own output: every other list in standupText has a cap and an "…and N more" line — review 5 (standup.mjs:55), backlog 3 (:60), open STANDUP_OPEN (:82), decisions STANDUP_DECISIONS (:88). The shipped-in-7-days loop at standup.mjs:70 has neither, and on this board it printed 38 lines — 2,700 of the standup’s 4,574 chars, i.e. the majority of what a session is handed unasked.

Not a runaway: the window is 7 days, so it is bounded by throughput, not by time, and a quiet week costs nothing. But it is the one section whose size a burst week decides, and it is the least decision-relevant thing in the report — a session needs to know what it must not reverse and what is unresolved far more than it needs 38 titles of finished work.

Fix is the same shape as its four neighbours: a cap plus the "…and N more" line the others already carry. Deliberately P3 — this is a tidy-up, not a cost the way SW-039/040/041 are.

MEASURED 2026-07-31 against this repo’s own memory (117 entries): mcp.mjs:330 renders each hit with line(e) and no max, so the COUNT is clamped to 50 (mcp.mjs:312) while the BYTES are not. recall({kind:"finding", limit:50}) returns 37,013 chars ≈ 9.3k tokens in a single tool result; kind:"outcome" 10,623 chars; kind:"decision" 7,754. The default limit of 10 keeps the common case near 2k, so this bites exactly when a session raises the limit — i.e. when it is hunting for something and least wants its context eaten.

standup already has the answer: line(e, {max}) and excerpt() are shared code this caller simply does not use. Fix is a max that tightens as the hit count rises, plus keeping the "raise limit to see them" hint honest by reporting that entries were CLIPPED as well as dropped.

SHIPPED on chore/bound-memory-reads (a116bf2). recall clamped how MANY entries came back (50) but never how long they were, because line() was called with no max while standup passed 240/200. Entries now share ONE budget (RECALL_BUDGET 9000 chars in standup.mjs) and each takes a share of it, floored at 320 and ceilinged at 1600 — a flat per-entry clip would be too mean for one hit and too generous for fifty. The floor deliberately wins over the budget: fifty entries clipped to 180 chars each is fifty entries that say nothing, and a caller only reaches fifty by explicitly asking.

FOUND WHILE FIXING IT, and fixed in the same card: the "files:" line was unbounded too — refs() pulls every path an entry names, and a note surveying a subsystem names dozens, so a text-only budget would have leaked straight through it. fileList() bounds it to 200 chars keeping WHOLE names, because a path clipped mid-segment is not a shorter path, it is a wrong one.

Clipped and dropped are reported as the different losses they are: one is an entry you never saw, the other an entry you saw the point of. Reporting only "…N more" while silently truncating the rest would make the answer read as complete.

MEASURED, old server vs new against this repo's own tracker (120 entries), same document: recall(finding,50) 37,685 → 9,740 chars (9.4k → 2.4k tokens); recall(outcome,50) 10,985 → 7,311; recall(decision,50) 8,544 → 6,283; recall(file:"shipward/mcp.mjs",6) 8,777 → 6,859.

TEST NOTE for whoever reads mcp.test.mjs next: "a reply larger than the pipe buffer is not truncated when stdin closes" (the SW-005 flush bug) built its >64KiB frame out of recall({kind:'finding',limit:50}). This card made that impossible, so the test was silently no longer testing the flush — it now builds the frame from standup's working-card titles, which are unclipped and uncapped. The assertion did not change; the vehicle did. If SW-042 ever caps that list, this test needs a new vehicle again.

261 tests pass, 9 new (4 in memory.test.mjs for noteDigest, 5 in mcp.test.mjs over the real pipe).

MEASURED 2026-07-31: mcp.mjs:398 renders the handoff with noteText(card.note) and no clip, unlike standup, which passes a max to excerpt() (standup.mjs:82 uses 240, :88 uses 200). Biggest notes today — CA-011 6,187 chars ≈ 1.5k tokens, CA-013 5,511, SW-024 4,873 — and a card that is started repeatedly grows without bound. start() sits on the mandatory protocol path (CLAUDE.md rule 2), so every task pays this.

The machinery already exists: excerpt(entry, max) in public/memory-lib.js:191 leads with the point via pointIndex() instead of the preamble. The judgement call is that start() is the one surface where a session legitimately wants the WHOLE note — it is about to work that card. So the likely shape is: keep the most recent N entries in full, clip the older ones, and SAY how many were clipped and that recall reaches them. A silent truncation here would be worse than the tokens, for the same reason recall reports its dropped count.

SHIPPED on chore/bound-memory-reads (a116bf2). start() now renders the note through noteDigest() instead of noteText(): the newest 3 entries exactly as before — that is the state a session is resuming and it should arrive whole — and everything older clipped to 400 chars through the same excerpt() standup already used, which leads with the point rather than the preamble. The reply says how many entries were clipped.

DECISION worth not reversing: the pointer for the full note is the desk and .shipward/tracker.json, NOT recall. recall clips too (SW-041), so "call recall for the rest" would have been a promise this server cannot keep.

MEASURED, old server vs new against the same live documents: CA-011 6,187 → 4,265 chars (1,547 → 1,066 tokens, 4 entries clipped), CA-013 5,672 → 4,741, CA-012 4,513 → 3,754, SW-024 4,873 → 3,286.

KNOWN LIMIT, stated rather than hidden: a card whose newest 3 entries are themselves huge is still unbounded — SW-019, SW-015 and SW-020 have 3 or fewer entries and so clip to nothing, still handing back ~4,200 chars (~1k tokens). That is the design the card specified and it is defensible (you want the state you are resuming), but if start ever needs a hard ceiling, this is where it is missing. Also: noteText() now has no production caller — it survives as a public function of memory-lib with its own test, not as dead code, but nothing would break if the desk never picks it up.

MEASURED 2026-07-31 on this repo’s own board: .shipward/tracker.json is 138 KB across 38 cards (15 pushed, 23 shipped), and note text is 69% of those bytes (95 KB). A second onboarded board: 47 KB / 13 cards, notes 73%. Cards are never deleted by protocol and notes are append-only, so the hot file only grows — nothing does for card notes what FEED_CAP + feed-archive.jsonl (tracker-store.mjs:65, :106) already do for the feed.

The cost is NOT the standup: that is capped by design (STANDUP_OPEN/STANDUP_DECISIONS, entries clipped to 240/200) and measures ~4.4k chars ≈ 1.1k tokens on this tracker, roughly flat as the board grows. The cost is the MCP-offline fallback CLAUDE.md documents as supported — "read → modify → write the whole file" — which is ~35k tokens to read and a full rewrite to save, scaling linearly with the file. It also makes git diff on the tracker unreadable, and the tracker is committed to git precisely so it can be recovered by hand (see the SW-033 clobber).

The design question to settle BEFORE code: where do shipped-card notes go, and how does recall still reach them? feed-archive.jsonl can be write-only because nothing ever reads it back; card notes cannot, because recall({file}) is the mandatory pre-edit step (CLAUDE.md rule 0) and a finding filed under a long-shipped card is exactly what it must still surface. So the archive needs a reader, or the split has to be by entry age/kind rather than by card status.

Alberto, on the desk: where is browser back? A desk opened from the fleet had no way home but browser chrome — invisible in the Claude Code pane. Fix: the fleet appends ?fleet=<its origin> to each desk link; the desk renders a home link in the header when, and only when, that param names a localhost origin. Validated by a pure lib function, because a URL taken from the query string and rendered as a link is exactly how open-redirect decorations get in.

SHIPPED. fleet.mjs stamps each desk link with ?fleet=<origin>; app.js reads it once through lib_s fleetLinkFrom(), which accepts ONLY http://localhost:port or http://127.0.0.1:port — javascript: urls, real domains, localhost.evil.com and path-carrying values all die in the test suite, because a link rendered from a query parameter is an open redirect wearing a home icon. A desk opened without the param (bookmark, manual serve) shows no link at all.

Deferred from SW-020, deliberately. notifications/cancelled is accepted and then ignored: the cancelled call keeps running, still writes, and still holds the write queue behind it. Real cancellation means carrying an AbortSignal from the notification through callTool into mutate() and the cross-process file lock, and deciding what a half-applied mutation means — a lock holder cannot simply be abandoned. That is a larger change than the finding warrants, and bodging it would be worse than the honest gap. The blast radius today is small: a client that cancels gets no reply and the write lands anyway.

IMPLEMENTED, and the deferral reasoning in the brief above turned out to be answerable rather than blocking. THE SHAPE: cancellation is best-effort with a DEFINED COMMIT POINT, which is the only honest version of it. A queued call never runs. A running one is abandoned inside mutate() just before the write, lock released and file untouched. While waiting for the lock, acquire() checks the signal on each retry, so a cancelled call stops occupying the write queue instead of blocking whatever is behind it — that was the part I had assumed needed a big change and did not. Past the rename the write is durable, so the work finishes; cancelling there would mean inventing an undo. Either way NO response is sent, per the protocol. DESIGN CALL: CancelledError is its own type, not a tool failure — nothing went wrong and nothing was written, so it must not surface as an errored result the model would read and retry. An unknown or already-finished requestId is ignored, because a reply and a cancellation crossing is the normal race. Edge Case Hunter over tracker-store.mjs. FIRST, THE FIX HOLDS: 1600/1600 writes landed with 0 lost, and 2083/2100 on a harder run where ~4 losses were expected at the old rate. The one-observation inspect() and link-a-complete-scratch publish() genuinely closed SW-010. TEN FINDINGS UNDER IT. F1 lost-write, SILENT: held() is checked before atomicWrite, but the commit is open+write+fsync+chmod+rename — measured p50 5.17ms and max 16.17ms on a realistic 43KB tracker, the same order as LOCK_RETRY_MS, not microseconds. A card vanished with no error raised anywhere. F2 corruption: breakLock renames the lock to a grave BEFORE checking the inode, so a third process can publish into the freed path and the link-back then unlinks that innocent holder lock; F2 is F1 trigger. F3 permanent deadlock: alive(pid) makes a lock unbreakable FOREVER — a lock 24h old held by pid 1 timed out at 60s and never becomes breakable. The lock lives in the repo working directory so it survives a reboot, after which the pid is very likely someone else. F4 permanent deadlock: release() swallows unlink errors, so one transient EACCES leaks a lock carrying a LIVE pid and wedges that daemon for its whole lifetime. F5 permanent deadlock: age<0 means NEW with no upper bound, so an mtime one hour in the future is immortal and any backwards clock step immortalizes every existing lock. F6: the heartbeat utimes a PATH, so a dispossessed holder keeps a corpse fresh forever and a third writer fails at 60s. F7: a provably dead holder still costs 30s, and LOCK_TIMEOUT is only 2x LOCK_STALE, so two crashes inside one waiter deadline is a guaranteed failure — 2 of 4 clean writers hard-failed. F8: no fairness, 17 of 2100 writes timed out and ALL 17 were the same starved process. F9: withLock is not re-entrant, a nested mutate is a silent 60s hang. F10: graves are never swept, neither sweep regex matches .lock.dead.<uuid>. NEGATIVE RESULTS WORTH KEEPING: 4000 create/delete cycles produced 4000 distinct inodes on APFS so the F2 guard is sound here, but ext4/HFS+ recycle aggressively and it would false-negative there; publish() partial writes are not reproducible; link() on FAT/network mounts is untested and would fail with a raw errno and no diagnosis.

FIXED, 9 of 10. THE PRINCIPLE THAT CHANGED: liveness is a hint, the heartbeat is the evidence. A living holder refreshes its mtime every second, so silence past LOCK_ABANDONED_MS (5 min) is abandonment whatever the pid says — that single reframing closed F3 (a live pid made a lock unbreakable FOREVER, and the lock survives a reboot after which the pid is someone else's) without reopening SW-010's slow-but-alive bug. F1, the silent lost write: held() now runs at the last instant before rename rather than before a 5-16ms commit, so nothing is published by a holder that no longer holds. F5: a future mtime is bounded at 5s — beyond that it is a broken clock, not sub-millisecond precision, and unbounded it made locks immortal. F7: a provably dead holder costs 2s not 30, because the pid check already proved it gone; at the old grace two crashes inside one waiter deadline was a guaranteed failure. F4: release retries and then warns loudly instead of swallowing. F2: breakLock re-reads and aborts if the lock is no longer the inode it condemned. F6: the heartbeat verifies the token before touching, so a dispossessed holder can no longer keep a corpse fresh. F9: a nested mutate throws immediately. F10: graves are swept on age. F8 partially — jittered backoff spreads the cost but is still not a queue; a true FIFO would need a ticket file and that is a bigger change than the starvation warrants. NEGATIVE RESULT WORTH KEEPING: the inode guard is sound on APFS (4000 create/delete cycles, 4000 distinct inodes) but ext4 and HFS+ recycle aggressively and it would false-negative there; link() on FAT or a network mount is untested and would fail with a raw errno and no diagnosis. 160 tests pass, 5 new. Contention stress re-run clean at 2700 writes with 0 lost.
Merged to main. F8 (fairness) is only partly addressed — jittered backoff spreads the starvation but is still not a queue. Named here rather than left implied.

The Blind Hunter BROKE the invariant I claimed for the status line, on its first try. FINDING 1, worst of the day: status.mjs interpolates card text straight into stdout with nothing stripped, so tracker data becomes terminal control. Proven with real output — a title containing \u001b]0;PWNED\u0007 rewrites the terminal/tab title, \u001b[2J\u001b[H clears the screen, \u001b[?1049h switches to the alternate screen buffer, a bare \r overwrites the line just drawn, and a newline turns a one-line status line into three. TITLE_BUDGET is no mitigation: the clear-screen payload is 7 characters. Worse, the card ID is never clipped at all and status.mjs never calls validate(), so ID_RE does not apply to it. U+202E RTL override passes through too. CLAUDE.md blesses hand-editing and log() takes free text, so this is data the tool invites. FINDING 2: emit() in the hooks writes then calls process.exit(0), which drops whatever has not flushed — a hard cliff at exactly 65536 bytes on a pipe. One card with a 70KiB title makes every hook emit unparseable truncated JSON, and past ~1000 cards the write is lost entirely so the STOP HOOK SILENTLY STOPS BLOCKING. It fails open, which is the wrong direction. FINDING 3: the stdin read has no timeout, so a pipe held open hangs the hook until the runtime kills it — on UserPromptSubmit that is a stall every single turn; 600MiB of stdin was also buffered in full. FINDING 4: the PreToolUse matcher includes NotebookEdit but the handler reads tool_input.file_path, and NotebookEdit passes notebook_path, so it can never warn. Also: clip() splits emoji into lone surrogates; openItems() does an uncapped memory scan on every render (390ms at 1000 cards); and activeLine() injects card text into the model context every turn with no framing that it is data.

FIXED. Every value that reaches the terminal is scrubbed of C0, DEL, C1, the bidi overrides and the line separators, and the card ID is now bounded like the title — it was neither clipped nor validated, since status.mjs never calls validate(). Hook output is bounded BEFORE the write and drained before exit: over the bound it says less correctly instead of more corruptly, and the Stop hook can no longer fall silent, which was how it failed OPEN. GOTCHA WORTH KEEPING: my first stdin-timeout fix used AbortSignal.timeout and did nothing — a for-await blocked on the next chunk never reaches a condition it could check; the stream has to be DESTROYED on a deadline. The regression test caught that, which is the only reason I know. SECOND GOTCHA, on the nose: the tool refused to run my own command for containing raw control characters while I was writing the tests for control characters — the payloads are now built from String.fromCharCode so no literal control byte exists in the repo. Also fixed: NotebookEdit was in the PreToolUse matcher but the handler only read tool_input.file_path while NotebookEdit passes notebook_path, so it could never warn; the open-item scan is skipped past 400 cards (390ms at 1000, 1.6s at 5000) rather than stalling the render; clips no longer split an emoji into a lone surrogate; and activeLine now labels card text as tracker data, because a card can be logged from an issue body and its title reached the model context unframed on every turn. 155 tests pass; 8 new, each verified to fail against the pre-fix code.

THE GAP, measured: the tracker holds 27 memory entries / 4044 words, and standup returns 0 of them. The only path back is start, one card at a time, so Claude retrieves memory about the ticket it is opening and never about the code it is about to touch. From the agent's side this store is write-only. FIX: (1) standup gains a bounded memory section — decisions not to reverse, and still-open items, each with its card id and date; (2) a new recall tool takes file / kind / query and returns the entries attached, ranked by what it would cost to miss. DESIGN RULES: every entry arrives with its date and card so a session can judge rather than believe; evidence is labelled as a claim about a PAST state, because 'tests pass' rots (45 was true this morning, it is 96 now); nothing is silently truncated — recall says what it dropped and how to get it. Standup stays readable: entries are clipped with the card id kept so the full text is one recall away.

SHIPPED. standup now carries a bounded memory section (still-open items + decisions not to reverse, each stamped with card and date, clipped so the full text is one recall away) and a new recall({file|kind|query}) tool retrieves the rest, ranked by what it would cost to miss, always reporting what it dropped. TWO THINGS THAT ONLY SHOWED UP ON REAL DATA: (1) BRIDGING FILE TO PROSE — SW-010's note, the most valuable in this repo, names NO file at all; it names isStale(), breakLock(), sweepTmp(), because that is how you write down what went wrong. recall({file}) therefore reads the file off disk and asks about every name declared inside it, not just the filename. Before the bridge, recall({file:'tracker-store'}) returned one irrelevant hit; after, six with both SW-010 findings ranked first. (2) DROPPING GENERIC NAMES — tracker-store.mjs declares 73 names and most are now()/read()/line(), so matching any of them returned the whole tracker and the top hits were unrelated. Tokens appearing across more than a quarter of the memory are now dropped before scoring, and entries rank by how many distinct names they match. GOTCHA IN THAT FIX: the share filter then ate EVERY token on a small corpus, because with two entries one hit is already 50 percent — recall returned nothing at all. Nothing counts as generic until it has turned up at least 4 times; regression test covers the young-repo case. Evidence entries are labelled 'as of then, not a claim about now' at the point of use, because '45 tests pass' was true this morning and is 112 now. REPRODUCED while fixing SW-009. The 12-writer store test fails about 1 run in 6 under full-suite load: 11 of 12 cards land, every child exits 0, nothing is logged. A high-cycle harness (6 processes x 150 mutations) loses ~1 write per 900 reliably. ROOT CAUSE: isStale() judges the lock from TWO separate observations of the path — readHolder() then lstat() — and the lock can be replaced between them. When readHolder() hits the lock in its momentary absence (normal, between one holder release and the next publish) it returns null, and lstat() then measures a DIFFERENT, brand-new lock. That new lock trips `if (age < 0) return true` — the line commented "clock skew: as broken as too old". Measured: st.mtimeMs carries sub-millisecond precision while Date.now() truncates to whole ms, so a freshly created lock reads as up to 0.62ms in the FUTURE in 1085 of 2000 observations. Over half of all new locks are therefore condemned the instant that race is hit. Trace confirms the full chain: break-won by a waiter, then 6ms later the true holder gets release-skip (its lock is gone) and its atomic-write chmod fails ENOENT because breakLock -> sweepTmp deleted the live holder’s in-flight .tmp. Two writers in the critical section, one write silently overwritten. THREE DEFECTS: (1) isStale reads stat and content from different observations; (2) age < 0 is treated as death when it actually means brand new; (3) sweepTmp unlinks temp and lock-scratch files belonging to LIVE processes.

FIXED. inspect() now reads mtime, inode and holder from ONE open handle, so a stat and a read can never land on two different locks. A future mtime means new, not dead (the old 'age < 0 = as broken as too old' line was the trigger). breakLock() compares the grave's inode against the snapshot it judged and puts an innocent lock back. sweepTmp() only collects files whose pid is dead. withLock() hands callers a held() guard checked immediately before the commit, so a lost lock raises LockLostError instead of overwriting whoever holds it now. EVIDENCE: before, ~1 write lost per 900 under sustained contention (2 of 4 trials) and the 12-writer test failed ~1 run in 6 under full-suite load; after, 12960 contended writes across 14 trials with zero lost and six consecutive clean suite runs. 49 tests pass. Three new regression tests were each run against the PREVIOUS store and all three fail there: future-dated lock read as a corpse, sweep eating a live process's in-flight temp, and a mid-write lock loss writing anyway.

FINDING, observed once on 2026-07-31 at 11:33 immediately after the SW-045 merge: `session-start FIXES what git can prove and only reports the rest` failed in a full-suite run, taking 7408ms. Three consecutive full runs before and after were 355/355 green, and the hooks file alone passes that test in ~467ms. So it is a FLAKE, but not a meaningless one. The hook's audit is bounded by AUDIT_BUDGET_MS = 2500 and returns NO_DRIFT on expiry — silence, deliberately, because a slow repository must never delay a session. The test asserts the audit DID fix something. On a loaded machine (this run raced a merge, a second worktree's session, and the git index churn from both) the audit exceeds its budget, correctly returns nothing, and the test correctly fails. The budget is therefore load-bearing in a test that never mentions it. FIX OPTIONS, none obviously right: raise the budget in the test environment via an env var and assert the fix deterministically; or split the test in two — one that the audit ran at all, one that its OUTPUT is correct when given unbounded time; or assert the disjunction honestly (fixed OR timed out) and lose most of the test's value. Prefer the second. DO NOT simply raise AUDIT_BUDGET_MS: 2500ms is a product decision about how long a session start may be delayed, and a test is not a reason to change it. Worth noting because a flake nobody wrote down is a flake that gets re-diagnosed from scratch every few months.

ROOT CAUSE: spawnCheck resolves on child.on('close'), and 'close' waits for the child's STDIO STREAMS to reach EOF, not for the child to exit. child.kill() signals only the direct child; its grandchildren survive, and they hold the inherited stdout/stderr pipe open. So the runner dies on time and the promise waits for whatever it spawned. `node --test` runs test files in WORKER PROCESSES, which makes the single check this project recommends — and the one setup.mjs will suggest to every onboarded repo — the exact shape that defeats the bound. Note this is NOT the slowness itself. The suite is healthy: 429/429 in 23s standalone, and 429/429 in 23s under the scrubbed check environment SW-050 introduced. TWO CANDIDATE FIXES, and they are complementary rather than alternatives:

FINDING, surfaced while fixing SW-054 and worth writing down even though nothing has gone visibly wrong yet.

The SessionStart hook bounds its git audit with Promise.race against AUDIT_BUDGET_MS = 2500 and renders NO_DRIFT when the budget expires. But Promise.race does not cancel the loser. reconcile() keeps running after the race resolves — it can still take the tracker lock and still write the board — while the hook goes on to emit its context and call process.exit(). So the write races the exit.

Two consequences, and the second is the one that matters:

  1. "The audit timed out" does NOT mean "nothing was written". A session can be told the board was not corrected and find it corrected anyway. That is a lie of omission rather than a corruption, but it is the exact class of thing this codebase refuses elsewhere — see NO_DRIFT's own comment, "we do not know must never render as nothing is wrong".

  2. process.exit() can land while mutate() is mid-flight. The tracker write itself is safe — atomicWrite renames a fully-written temp file, so there is no torn document — but the lock is left behind. That is survivable by design (a lock whose pid is dead is breakable after DEAD_GRACE_MS = 2000) and it is why nothing has broken. It still means the routine path can leave a lock for the next writer to clean up, on a hook that runs at the start of every session.

Not a data-loss bug, and NOT a reason to raise the budget. The honest fixes are (a) pass an AbortSignal into reconcile so the loser is actually cancelled at its commit point — mutate() already accepts one and already throws CancelledError before the write, so most of the machinery exists; or (b) await the in-flight reconcile before exiting, bounded, so the process does not leave while holding a lock. (a) is truer to the intent: the budget exists so a session is not DELAYED, not so a correction is abandoned halfway.

FOUND 2026-08-01 by chasing down two "the timeout did not bound it" reports that were both wrong. This is the real finding underneath SW-056.

TWICE a check was recorded as killed after roughly 18 minutes against a 120 second budget, and both times it was the LID:

  SW-050, Jul 31: ms 1110053. pmset: 16:16:25 Clamshell Sleep, "Entering Sleep state ... 1064 secs", DarkWake 16:34:19. 1110053ms - 1064s leaves ~46s of actual running.
  SW-056, Aug 1:  ms 1057254. pmset: 10:38:49 "Entering Sleep state ... 964 secs", DarkWake 10:54:53, verification stamped 10:54:55. Leaves ~93s of actual running.

TWO SEPARATE PROBLEMS, one cause — the code measures and schedules in wall clock across an interval in which nothing was running.

1. THE DURATION IS WRONG. spawnCheck reports Date.now() - started, which keeps counting while the machine sleeps. "Killed after 1110053ms" is off by more than an order of magnitude and it reads as an accusation against the timeout — it cost me a wrong root cause in the SW-056 brief, and it will cost the next reader the same. The note that carries it is the memory, so this is a false statement written permanently into the board. Fix: measure with a monotonic source that does not advance across sleep (performance.now(), or process.hrtime.bigint()), and keep Date.now() only for the timestamp of WHEN it ran.

2. THE CHECK IS KILLED ON WAKE. The timer's clock DID advance through the sleep, so the 120s budget expired while the check was suspended and the kill landed as soon as the machine came back — on a check that had used ~93s of its 120s. Closing your laptop mid-hand-back therefore fails the check and leaves the card in progress, which is exactly what happened here and is indistinguishable from a real timeout.

Both are honest-reporting problems rather than data problems, which is why P2 and not P1. But the doctrine in this repo is that a check reports what it PROVED — and "killed after 1110053ms" proves nothing except that someone shut a laptop.

Worth deciding, not just fixing: should a check that spanned a sleep be reported as timed out at all? "Absence of evidence" is the honest answer either way, but the reason should say "the machine slept" rather than "your check is slow", because those lead a reader to opposite actions. Detecting it is cheap — compare elapsed wall clock against elapsed monotonic time and the difference IS the sleep.

Every locked write now stamps a monotonic rev the STORE owns and journals {rev, etag, at, pid} to .shipward/last-write.json — untracked on purpose, because if git could revert the journal the evidence would vanish with the write it records. A file whose rev is below the journal's was rewritten by something that never took the lock: reads warn once per regression per process (the desk polls every 3s; one event must not become a scroll) and still serve — deliberately checking out an old board is legitimate — and the next write appends one durable feed entry, then stamps past both file and journal, which is exactly what retires the warning.

The feed entry's by is ABSENT: git authored the rewrite; charging claude or user with it would be the quiet misattribution this exists to end. FINDING, measured across four full-suite runs on 2026-08-11: two were red (485 pass / 2 fail in 219s, 486 / 1 fail in 119s) and two were green (487 / 0, twice, in ~20s). THE THREE: (1) verify.test 'the timeout bounds the run even when the check leaves a grandchild holding its stdout' asserts elapsed < 6000 for a 1000ms timeout whose real question is 'did it wait for the grandchild's 30000ms life' — a 6s ceiling on a box spawning three node processes under load is a coin flip, and the honest bound is anything well under 30000; it then polls only 100x20ms = 2s for the orphan to die. (3) mcp.test 'the dry run names which tier each finding is in' took 32.6s in a red run against ~1s healthy — it stages a git repo and handshakes a server, so under load it exceeds the client's call timeout. WHY IT MATTERS NOW rather than as a nuisance: the repo is about to be public and the first thing a stranger does is clone and run the suite, on a machine we do not control. THE MECHANISM. spawnCheck resolves the outcome on 'exit' and then waits OUTPUT_GRACE_MS=250 for the rest of the output, resolving early if 'close' arrives. finish() then DESTROYS both pipes. So any byte still sitting in the OS pipe buffer when that timer fires is gone. On the ordinary path 'close' follows 'exit' almost immediately and the timer never matters — which is exactly why 250ms was fine everywhere it was measured, and why a 2-core runner is the first machine where it is not. FIX, and it is a real one rather than a test tweak: raise OUTPUT_GRACE_MS to 1000. It costs NOTHING on the ordinary path, because 'close' resolves first there; it is only ever paid when an orphan is holding the pipe open, which is the pathological case the bound exists for, and 750ms more on a check that already ran for seconds is not a cost worth defending. What it buys is margin on every slow or contended machine a real user might run on — the truncated output IS the note a human reads when a check fails, so losing the tail loses the summary. AND, following SW-065 rather than inventing something: give this test the same tooBusyToTime probe its sibling already uses. On a machine that cannot schedule the window, the test cannot tell 'the product truncated' from 'the OS did not run us', and a test that cannot distinguish those is measuring the machine. Skip with the probe time named, never relax the assertion. WORTH SAYING PLAINLY: this is a REAL limitation, not just a flaky test. The wait for trailing output is bounded, so on a sufficiently starved machine a check's last line can be dropped. The bound is deliberate — SW-056 chose a bounded truncation over an unbounded hang — and raising it widens the margin without changing that trade.

BRIEF. Second CI failure, different job (macos-latest/node 20), different test: 'contended breaking of one stale lock still admits only one writer'. Four processes race to break one dead lock; on the runner, one lost the lock mid-write and exited 1 with LockLostError. The test asserts all four writes land, so a lost writer fails it — correctly, because a write really did not happen. THE PRODUCT SIDE IS THE INTERESTING HALF. LockLostError's own guarantee is 'nothing was written'. That makes it precisely an optimistic-lock loss, and the right response to one is to run the transform again against a fresh read — not to hand the caller an exception and let them work out that their work is gone. Before this, four writers racing a dead lock landed three writes and one exception, and unless that caller thought to retry, its work simply vanished. So: mutate retries, bounded at 4 attempts with jittered backoff, ONLY on LockLostError. Validation failures, cancellations and etag conflicts are answers rather than accidents and are never repeated. Safe because fn is already contracted as a pure transform of the document it is handed — which is why done() runs its check OUTSIDE the lock (SW-043). CI is the verification, because a 2-core runner is the only machine this project has that can produce the race at all. FINDING, and a reversal. I built the retry described in the brief, and then reverted it. Two reasons, and the second is the one that matters. (1) It broke a test that is right. 'a holder that loses its lock mid-write writes nothing and says so' has a callback that STEALS its own lock, so every retry stole it again; the fourth attempt then waited out LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS and the case took 60s and produced the wrong error. (2) That test's comment states the design decision I was overriding: 'Defence in depth. Every known way to lose a lock is closed; if one is ever reopened, the symptom must be a loud error, not a vanished card.' Converting that loud error into a silent retry is against the grain of this whole codebase, and I was proposing it on the strength of a failure I could not reproduce even once in 55 trials across four configurations. THE ACTUAL RACE, which is what the next attempt should start from. The lock is broken by RENAME, which makes stealing a dead lock one atomic step — two breakers cannot both win and then delete each other's fresh lock. What rename does NOT do is make the break conditional on the lock still being the one the breaker observed. So: B reads the dead lock and judges it stale; A breaks it and publishes its own; B's rename then lands ON TOP of A's live lock; A's held() sees a token that is not its own and correctly refuses to write. The window is between B's observation and B's rename, and on a 2-core runner under four test workers that window is wide. Every guarantee in the header held; the gap is that 'break by rename' is atomic in the wrong dimension. THE SHAPE OF A REAL FIX is a conditional publish rather than an unconditional rename — link() is already imported here and is the atomic create-if-absent primitive: break by unlinking the OBSERVED inode and creating the new lock with link(), so a breaker whose observation is stale fails to create and loops instead of clobbering a live holder. That is a careful change to the most safety-critical file in the project and it deserves its own session with a reproduction harness, not the tail of a long one. NOT MAKING THE TEST TOLERANT, deliberately. Best-of-N is a valid pattern for a POSSIBILITY claim — verify.test.mjs uses it to prove the grace window CAN catch a post-exit line — and it is never valid for a SAFETY claim. 'No writer loses its write' cannot be established by passing on one attempt in five, and a test relaxed that way would hide exactly the defect it was written to catch. So CI stays red on this one job until the race is actually fixed, and that is the honest state of it rather than a fixture problem.

From a dev.to comment on the launch post. The suggestion: bind every successful check to the exact tree it evaluated (commit hash, command, exit code, output digest), and for dirty worktrees either refuse completion or hash the relevant files before and after the check and fail if they changed. Their invariant is worth keeping verbatim: not "this command passed" but "this command passed against the exact artifact now being marked complete".

Most of it already holds, and the reply said so. verificationOf records argv, exit, ms, sha and dirty; the verdict entry is anchored to verdict.sha rather than HEAD at write time, precisely because those diverge when something commits between the run and the write. The stale-result path they feared is closed a step earlier still: the agent never carries a result at all, because done() runs the check itself before taking the lock (mcp.mjs:589).

What does NOT hold is the half they found. runCheck calls headState ONCE, before the run (verify.mjs:406), and never again. A tree mutated DURING the check — another session, an editor save, a watcher, or a check that writes files itself — is recorded against the pre-run sha and the pre-run dirty flag. A check allowed 120s can therefore carry a clean sha for a tree that was not clean when it finished, which is the one thing the sha exists to rule out.

The fix is theirs: sample before and after, and say so when they differ. The open question is what a difference should COST. Refusing the promotion treats it as a failed check; recording it treats it the way dirty is treated now. Decide that before writing it, because it is the same argument as the sibling card: an override nobody can find is indistinguishable from a check that passed.

Output digest is the other half of their suggestion and is not filed here — see the sibling card about output on a pass.
